sections.title: The Prohibition of Bread
sections.html:
The purpose of the decree prohibiting the bread of gentiles (pat goyim) and the prohibition of food cooked by gentiles (bishulei goyim) is one – to prevent assimilation; however, in halakha there are differences between them. On the one hand, one is more stringent regarding bread, for even if it is of an inferior kind, it is forbidden because of its importance. However, in most of the laws, because of the great need a person has for bread, one is more lenient regarding bread. Therefore, in a time of pressing need, in a place where there are no Jewish bakers, one may be lenient and buy "pat palter" (bread of a professional baker) from gentile bakers (as explained in the next halakha).

The forbidden bread is bread that was baked by a gentile, whether he baked it in his home for his family or baked it in a bakery in order to sell it to the public. Even the inferior bread of the poor, which is never served at a respectable meal, as long as it is made from the five species of grain, has the importance of bread, which is a person's staple food, and the prohibition of gentile bread applies to it (SA 112:1). But breads made from kinds of legumes, such as corn and rice, have the law of a gentile's cooked dish, and therefore if they are fit to be served at a respectable meal, they are forbidden because of bishulei goyim. And if not, they are not subject to the prohibition of bishulei goyim.

Baked goods over which one usually recites "Mezonot", such as cakes and crackers, since they are defined as bread with regard to the mitzva of separating ḥalla, also have the law of bread, and they are forbidden to eat even when it is not customary to serve them at a respectable meal (above 11:10-12).

If a Jew participated in baking the bread, the bread is not considered gentile bread and it is permitted to eat it. Therefore, if a Jew lit the oven, or put the dough into it, or stirred the coals, or even only added a small chip of wood to the oven, or even lowered and raised the flame of the gas or the electric oven – the bread is kosher. For the main thing is that the Jewish people know that gentile bread is forbidden to them, and as long as they are careful that a Jew participates in some way in baking the bread, there is already a distinguishing sign for the Jewish people that they must preserve their distinctiveness, and the bread is permitted (Avoda Zara 38b; Rambam; SA 112:9; Levush).1

sections.title: The Permission of Pat Palter (Bread of a Professional Baker)
sections.html:
From the time the Sages decreed a prohibition on gentile bread, many Jews found it difficult to keep the decree, since bread is very much needed for sustaining life, and not every person can prepare for himself a large oven for baking bread. And although even a lesser court can annul a decree that did not spread among the Jewish people, the Sages did not annul the decree on bread, since it was accepted with great force, and in practice there were also many Jews who kept it. However, from time to time, when they saw how difficult it was to keep the decree on bread, they said things from which it can be inferred that it would have been fitting to annul it or to restrict it. Thus it is related in the name of Rabbi (the editor of the Mishna) that once, when he was in the field, a gentile brought before him fine bread, and he said: "How fine this bread is! What did the Sages see to forbid it?" And another time, when he came to a certain place and saw that bread was scarce for the students, he wondered: "Is there no palter here?" A palter is a nahtom, that is, one whose livelihood is baking breads. And they were uncertain whether he meant to say that it would be fitting to permit the bread of a gentile palter in a place where there is no Jewish baker, because with the bread of a palter the concern for becoming close is reduced, since the palter does not give his breads for free as an expression of personal closeness but sells them to the public for payment (Avoda Zara 35b).

Similarly, it is related (ibid. 37a) about his grandson, Rabbi Yehuda Nesi'a, that after he and his court permitted the decree on oil (above 27:5), he was asked whether he would also permit the decree on bread, for it was known that his opinion inclined that way. He replied that he would not permit bread, because he had already permitted two decrees, and it is not fitting for one court to permit three decrees, for one who permits three decrees is called "beit dina sharya" (a permissive court). And thus the decree on bread remained unclear (Yerushalmi Avoda Zara 2:8).

In practice, in a place where there is no Jewish baker, one may buy bread from a gentile palter, on condition that it is known that all of the bread's ingredients are kosher. But in a place where a Jewish baker is available, as in the State of Israel, there is no permission to buy bread from a gentile baker (SA 112:2).2

sections.title: The Parameters of the Permission
sections.html:
Outside the Land, in a place where it is difficult to obtain Jewish bread and also difficult to arrange for a Jew to light the baking oven on a regular basis, those who wish to be lenient may buy breads baked by a gentile palter, since with the bread of a palter there is not so much concern for drawing hearts close, as the palter bakes in order to sell to the public. As is the law for bread, so is the law for cakes and all baked goods made from the five species of grain, on condition that all of their ingredients are kosher.

If the palter baked breads for his household – they are forbidden. If an ordinary person baked breads in order to sell them to the public – they are permitted, for everything follows the intention of the baking (Rashba; Beit Yosef; Rema 112:2; SA 7; Shakh 11).

A place in which, because of pressing need, it was permitted to eat the bread of a gentile palter, and a Jewish baker arrived there – the permission is annulled. But if the Jewish baker cannot supply all the needs of the community, or the gentile's breads are better, it is permitted to continue buying from the gentile. Even when the Jewish baker's breads are good, but he does not have all the kinds of bread and baked goods, it is permitted to buy what he does not have from the gentile baker (SA 112:4-5; Knesset Ha-gedola). However, when in general the Jewish bakers supply all the needs of the community, even though in certain respects the gentiles' baked goods are better or have a certain distinctiveness, one should not be lenient and eat from them, since there is no need for it, only indulgence. Therefore, throughout the Land of Israel, it is forbidden to eat the bread and baked goods of gentiles, since Jewish kinds of breads and baked goods are available in abundance.

The permission to eat the bread and baked goods of a gentile palter is on condition that all the ingredients from which they were prepared are kosher. In the past, people generally knew from what ingredients each baked good was prepared, and therefore every Jew could know whether the baked good that the gentile palter had prepared was made from kosher ingredients. However, today, bread and other baked goods are composed of dozens of ingredients intended to improve the taste, enhance the rising, beautify the baked good, extend its shelf life and the like. These ingredients may be made from the fats of pigs or of calves that were not slaughtered according to halakha, or may have been produced from insects (below 37:1-5). Therefore, the permission to eat the bread of a gentile palter outside the Land today is on condition that it was checked and found that all the ingredients from which he prepared his baked goods are kosher. Since a private individual generally does not know how to check this, in a place where there is a need to permit the bread and baked goods of a gentile palter, rabbis from the area must check this and, to the extent possible, rule that it is permitted.

sections.title: The Customs of Those Who Are Stringent, and the Law for Those Traveling Abroad
sections.html:
Even outside the Land, in places where most of the public was accustomed to be lenient and eat the bread of a gentile palter, there were many who were meticulous and were stringent with themselves not to eat the bread of a gentile palter. However, for a great or important need, such as for a Shabbat meal, even the meticulous were accustomed to be lenient and eat the bread of a gentile palter.

When one who is meticulous not to eat the bread of a gentile palter hosts at his table a guest who is not meticulous about this, in a place where the custom is that the host recites the blessing over the bread and breaks it for the guest as well, as long as the gentile's bread is finer than the Jew's bread, out of respect for the guest and the mitzva of hospitality, he should break the gentile's bread, and since he has already begun eating from it after the blessing, he is permitted to eat from it throughout the meal (SA 112:13). But in a place where the custom is that each person recites the blessing for himself, as many are accustomed today, the host should recite the blessing over Jewish bread, and let the guest recite the blessing over the fine gentile bread (MB 168:21).

If one who is careful about gentile bread dines together with friends who are not careful, as long as their gentile bread is finer, he is permitted to eat gentile bread with them, so that he will not appear to be holding himself above them with his stringency and harm the good relations that should prevail between them (Rema 112:15; Shakh 21).

When a person who is meticulous not to eat gentile bread did not manage to obtain Jewish bread for himself, if he can obtain Jewish bread by walking or traveling for 18 minutes (the measure of walking a mil), he should take the trouble to bring it. If it is farther away, he is permitted to eat gentile bread. And if he is on the road, if he knows that within 72 minutes further along his way he will be able to obtain Jewish bread, he should wait until he buys Jewish bread. If he would have to wait longer, he may eat gentile bread (SA 112:16; Pitḥei Teshuva 6; Peninei Halakha: Tefilla 2:4, n. 4).

As is the law for those who are stringent outside the Land, so is the law for Israelis who travel abroad: they are considered like those who are stringent about gentile bread, and in a time of need they are permitted to be lenient.3

The poskim recommended that even those who are lenient about gentile bread should conduct themselves like those who are stringent at least during the Ten Days of Repentance (SA OḤ 603:1).

sections.title: Bishulei Goyim (Food Cooked by Gentiles)
sections.html:
An additional safeguard that the Sages established for the Jewish people to keep them from assimilating among the gentiles is the prohibition of bishulei goyim (above 27:6). That is, even when there is no kashrut problem at all with the foods or with the pots in which they were cooked, it is forbidden for a Jew to eat dishes that a gentile cooked. Included in the prohibition of cooking are all foods prepared for eating by means of the heat of fire or electricity, including those fried in deep oil in a pot or in a little oil in a frying pan, roasted over fire, or baked or toasted in an oven. Likewise foods cooked by steam or in a microwave or in any manner in which it is customary to use heat to cook. But foods prepared by gentiles by salting, pickling or cold smoking are permitted (SA 113:13).4

The prohibition of bishulei goyim applies to dishes that have a certain importance, which a person can serve at a respectable meal, and consequently they may lead to drawing hearts close. But with simple foods, there is not so much concern for drawing close, since the cooking was not significant for them, and therefore they are not subject to the prohibition. The Sages stated two rules in defining important dishes: the first, that they are not eaten raw as they are, but rather it is the cooking that makes them fit for eating. For example, milk and its products are eaten raw, and therefore they are not subject to the prohibition of bishulei goyim, whereas meat and flour are not eaten raw, and therefore their cooking is subject to the prohibition. The second rule, that they are served at a king's table to accompany bread; but if they are dishes that only simple people are accustomed to eat, they are not subject to the prohibition. The first rule is the main one in practice, because it is the one that determines the law of most foods, whereas the second rule pertains to individual foods, because today, thanks to variety and openness, almost all kinds of food are served at a king's table.5

sections.title: The First Rule – They Are Not Eaten Raw
sections.html:
The first rule in the prohibition of bishulei goyim is that it concerns a food that people are not accustomed to eat raw. That is, a food that cooking makes fit for eating, and consequently the cooking is significant for it. Therefore, there is a prohibition on dishes of meat and fish, since they are not eaten raw. Likewise there is a prohibition on dishes of grain and flour, such as groats, ptitim and noodles. And likewise on dishes of legumes, such as lentils, chickpeas and rice. And even a food that can be eaten raw in a time of pressing need, such as an egg, which can be swallowed raw, is subject to the prohibition of bishulei goyim (Avoda Zara 38b; SA 113:14-15).

Milk and all its products, such as cheese and butter, are not subject to the prohibition of bishulei goyim, since they are eaten raw without cooking. And although today it is customary to heat milk for pasteurization (to disinfect it of bacteria), since the intention of pasteurization is not to improve its taste, the milk is considered as eaten raw.

Fruit is not subject to the prohibition, since it is customary to eat it raw. Therefore, fruit jam is not subject to the prohibition. Likewise, spices are not subject to the prohibition, since it is customary to mix them into foods that are eaten raw as well, such as salad (MB 203:11).

Most vegetables are not subject to the prohibition, since they are eaten raw. Therefore, matbuḥa salad is not subject to the prohibition, since its ingredients, which are tomatoes, peppers and onions, are eaten raw. But there are vegetables that in many places people are not accustomed to eat raw, such as potatoes, zucchini, beets and eggplants, and consequently they are subject to the prohibition of bishulei goyim. However, one in whose environment people eat these vegetables raw as well, for example by mixing slices of them into a salad, is not subject to the prohibition of bishulei goyim with them. And even though he and his family members are not accustomed to eat them raw, since he knows that many in his environment sometimes eat them raw, for him too they are considered foods that are eaten raw. But if he only heard that there are some who eat them raw, they are subject to the prohibition of bishulei goyim for him.

Determining the status of a food, whether it is eaten raw, depends on its state before cooking. For example, in the past people were accustomed to eat raw wheat kernels, and therefore if they were cooked – they were not subject to the prohibition. But if the wheat was ground into flour, since flour is not eaten raw, every dish made from it was forbidden. And today people are not accustomed to eat raw wheat kernels, and they too are subject to the prohibition. Fish and meat that were salted until they became fit for eating, if afterwards a gentile cooked them, they are not subject to the prohibition, since already before the cooking they were fit for eating (SA 113:12).6

If things that are eaten raw, such as cheese and vegetables, and things that are not eaten raw, such as flour and egg, were mixed in one dish, one follows the main ingredient, according to which the blessing is also determined (SA 113:2).

sections.title: The Second Rule – Served at a King's Table
sections.html:
The second rule is that the food "is served at a king's table to accompany bread." "A king's table" means a meal of distinguished people, and "to accompany bread" means that it is eaten as part of a meal, either as the main part of the meal in order to be satiated, or as a tasty food that it is customary to serve as dessert at the end of the meal. That is, even a dish of a food that is not eaten raw, if it is not customary to eat it as part of a respectable meal, is not subject to the prohibition of bishulei goyim. And everything is according to time and place. Therefore, in our times, as a result of the enormous variety of foods and the openness to different kinds of cuisine, all the foods that people are accustomed to serve at a meal can be served at a king's table. And even a person who is not accustomed to serve a particular dish at a respectable meal, as long as he knows that in his environment it is sometimes customary to serve it, it is subject to the prohibition of bishulei goyim for him.

However, foods that are not intended for eating or for dessert as part of a meal, such as candies, chocolate, kinds of roasted seeds and nuts (pitzuḥim) and other snacks, are not subject to the prohibition of bishulei goyim.

Breakfast cereals and rice cakes are subject to the prohibition of bishulei goyim, since it is customary to eat them to satiety at breakfast.

Coffee and alcoholic beverages are not subject to the prohibition of bishulei goyim, since they are intended for drinking and they consist mainly of water, which people are accustomed to drink raw. The proof is that over coffee one recites "Shehakol" and not "Ha-etz," the blessing over coffee beans, and over vodka and beer one recites "Shehakol" and not "Ha-adama," the blessing over the grain kernels from which they are prepared (Tosafot Avoda Zara 31b, s.v. "Ve-tarvayhu"; Taz 114:1). And some added another reason for permitting it, that coffee and tea are not necessarily served as part of the meal (Pri Ḥadash 6; Zera Emet OḤ 41).7

sections.title: Participation of a Jew Permits
sections.html:
When a Jew is a partner in the cooking, and even if he helped it only slightly, for example by improving it through stirring its contents while it was cooking, the dish is kosher. All the more so the dish is kosher if the Jew placed it on the fire, or lit the fire under it, or raised it in a manner that helps the cooking (SA 113:6-7).8

Regarding bread we learned (in halakha 1) that even participation in lighting the fire before the baking begins is effective in rendering kosher the bread that was afterwards baked by a gentile; however, regarding cooking there is a disagreement. Some are lenient and hold that the law of a cooked dish is like the law of bread, and whenever a Jew added a chip of wood to the fire on which the dish will afterwards be cooked, or slightly lowered the gas flame and raised it again, since he was a partner in kindling the fire, all the dishes that the gentile will afterwards cook on that fire will be kosher. And this is the custom of those of Ashkenazi descent.

And some are stringent and hold that only regarding bread were they lenient in this, since it is very much needed by a person, but regarding a cooked dish, only the participation of a Jew at the time of the cooking itself, by placing the dish on the fire, or by adding fire under it in a manner that helps it, renders it kosher. And this is the custom of those of Sephardic descent (SA 113:7).

For example, when frying an omelet or meat in a frying pan, according to the lenient opinion a Jew may light the fire under the frying pan, and afterwards a gentile may fry on it many omelets or pieces of meat for hours. And according to the stringent opinion, throughout the entire frying it must be a Jew who places the omelets or pieces of meat on the frying pan, because lighting the fire under the frying pan is effective only for the food that is on it at that time.

Since today members of all communities live together, and members of the Eastern and North African communities were accustomed to be stringent, even though the law is rabbinic, ab initio one should rule for members of all communities according to the stringent opinion. And after the fact, since the law is rabbinic, one should rule for members of all communities according to the permissive opinion. And in places where there is no personal closeness between the cook and the diners, such as in a public kitchen or in a restaurant where the cook does not go out to the diners, one may ab initio grant regular kashrut certification according to the lenient opinion, but "mehadrin" certification may be granted only to those who follow the stringent opinion.9

sections.title: Commercial and Public Cooking, and Hired Workers in a Jewish Home
sections.html:
Some say that just as they were lenient in a time of need to buy bread from a gentile palter, since there is not so much drawing close with baked goods baked for many people, so too one should be lenient with a gentile who cooks for the public, such as a cook in a restaurant who has no connection with the diners, that in a time of need his dishes are permitted (Maharitatz). However, according to most poskim, the permission of "pat palter" is specific to bread, on which life depends, but regarding cooked foods the Sages made no distinction in their decree, and the prohibition applies whether the cooking is done in a home kitchen or in a commercial or public kitchen. However, in a time of need, when there are additional reasons to be lenient, one may rely on the lenient opinion in this.

One opinion holds that the prohibition applies when the gentile cooks in his own home, but if he cooks in a Jewish home, there is no prohibition. In practice the poskim ruled that the prohibition applies even when the gentile cooks in a Jewish home.10

sections.title: The Sick and Those Requiring Nursing Care
sections.html:
A sick person who needs a cooked dish on Shabbat, even though his illness is not dangerous, it is permitted to ask a gentile to cook a dish for him. This is because the prohibition of asking a gentile to perform melakha on Shabbat is rabbinic, and for a sick person the Sages permitted their prohibitions (Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 28:2). Included in the permission to ask a gentile to cook on Shabbat for a sick person, they also permitted the sick person to eat from the gentile's dish (Ran and Levush).

If some of the dish remained for Motza'ei Shabbat, some say that even healthy people are permitted to eat from it, since it was cooked with permission for the sick person (Ra'ah and Rema 113:16). And some say that on Motza'ei Shabbat even the sick person himself is forbidden to eat from the dish that the gentile cooked for him, since now a Jew can cook the foods he needs (Rashba and Ran). And this is the opinion of most Aḥaronim (Taz 15, Pri Ḥadash, Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav, Pri To'ar, Ḥokhmat Adam, Ben Ish Ḥai, Year Two, Ḥukat 25).

An elderly or sick person who needs a gentile caregiver to look after him, as long as the person being cared for is able to light the fire on which the gentile will cook, or the oven in which the gentile will bake or roast, he must exert himself and take the trouble to do so. And if he cannot, it is a mitzva for his children and family members to exert themselves as much as they can to prepare dishes for him and place them in his refrigerator, and the gentile will heat them for him. In a time of pressing need, when the elderly or sick person has no relatives or friends who can bring him dishes cooked by Jews, since he is sick and greatly needs this, he may rely on the opinion of the few who are lenient in this. But his family members and visitors are forbidden to eat from those dishes.11

sections.title: The Law of the Utensils
sections.html:
Utensils in which a gentile cooked dishes, even though all the ingredients of the dish were kosher – the utensils require kashering, for whatever the Sages forbade, they forbade similar to a Torah prohibition, and just as utensils in which Torah prohibitions were cooked require kashering, so utensils in which rabbinic prohibitions were cooked require kashering (Rashba and Ran). And some say that the utensils do not require kashering, since the basis of the prohibition of bishulei goyim is lest they come to drawing close and intermarriage, and from the taste absorbed in and adhering to the utensils there is no concern for drawing close (Rosh and Ra'ah).

In practice the halakha follows the stringent opinion, and the utensil in which the gentile cooked requires kashering by hagala (purging in boiling water) or libun (heating with fire). But after the fact, if they transgressed and cooked in the utensil without kashering, the dish is permitted. However, the utensil is still forbidden for use, since it has not yet been kashered.12

If the utensil in which the gentile cooked was earthenware, it is kashered by hagala three times. And although if other forbidden foods were cooked in it, according to the overwhelming majority of poskim an earthenware utensil may not be kashered by hagala, regarding the prohibition of bishulei goyim, whose basis is rabbinic, one relies on those who hold that an earthenware utensil can be kashered by hagala three times (SA 113:16; see above 32, n. 4).
